title: How Much Exercise You Actually Need
hook: The headline number is smaller than most people fear: about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week — roughly 20-some minutes a day — moves the needle on your health.
key_points: Adults should aim for 150–300 minutes of moderate, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous, activity weekly.
Add muscle-strengthening work on two or more days a week for full benefit.
Any movement counts and beats none — short bouts through the day add up.
Sitting less and moving more lowers the risk of heart disease, diabetes, and several cancers.
content_html: How much exercise do you need to be healthier? Less than the gym makes it feel. The World Health Organization's guidance for adults lands at about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week — a brisk walk most days gets you there.
extra_html: The WHO recommends that adults do 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity each week, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity, plus muscle-strengthening work on two or more days. "Moderate" means you can talk but not sing — brisk walking, cycling, or housework all qualify. Crucially, the WHO stresses that any amount beats none, and that activity can be banked in short chunks rather than one long session. Hitting these levels is linked to lower rates of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, several cancers, and depression, and to better sleep and balance. The other half of the message is to sit less: prolonged sitting carries its own risks, which more movement helps offset.

related.title: Why Strength Training Matters
related.hook: Cardio gets the glory, but lifting, resistance bands, and bodyweight moves protect something running can't: the muscle and bone you'll rely on for decades.

related.title: Preventing Type 2 Diabetes
related.hook: Type 2 diabetes often arrives slowly, with a warning stage called prediabetes — and at that stage, modest lifestyle changes can stop or delay it.

related.title: Staying Strong as You Age
related.hook: The decline we associate with old age is partly the result of doing less. Staying active — in four distinct ways — keeps you independent far longer.

flashcards.prompt: How much moderate-intensity activity does the WHO recommend for adults each week?
flashcards.explanation_html: The WHO recommends 150–300 minutes of moderate activity per week — or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity — for substantial health benefits.

flashcards.prompt: Besides cardio, what else does the WHO say adults should do weekly?
flashcards.back_html: Muscle-strengthening activities on two or more days a week, working all the major muscle groups.

flashcards.prompt: If you can't hit the full weekly target, is some activity still worth it?
flashcards.back_html: Yes — the WHO is clear that some physical activity is better than none, and even short bouts spread through the day count toward the total.
